doc_title: Evaluation of certain food additives: one-hundredth report of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (WHO Technical Report Series 1058)
publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 1. Introduction
text:
The One-hundredth meeting of the Joint Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)/World Health Organization (WHO) Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) met in Rome from 10 to 19 June 2025.1 The meeting was opened on behalf of the FAO by Ms Angeliki Vlachou, Food Safety Officer, Agrifood Systems and Food Safety Division, and on behalf of WHO by Dr Moez Sanaa, Head of Standards and Scientific Advice on Food and Nutrition, Department on Nutrition and Food Safety.

Ms Vlachou welcomed the participants of the One-hundredth JECFA to the meeting on behalf of FAO by noting that the spirit of the Committee’s work is perfectly captured by the expression “quality is not an act, it is a habit”. Over the course of 100 meetings, JECFA has upheld a strong tradition of scientific excellence, transparency and integrity. Its consistent commitment to evidence-based evaluation has played a key role in shaping Codex Alimentarius standards, informing national policies and contributing to safer agrifood systems globally. Ms Vlachou emphasized that the centennial meeting was not simply a celebration of a single moment, but a recognition of JECFA’s long-standing habit of excellence. Since its establishment in 1956, the Committee has evolved to encompass scientific progress, respond to emerging challenges and maintain its trusted voice in global food safety. In closing, Ms Vlachou expressed sincere appreciation to all participants for their dedication, scientific expertise and collaborative spirit.

doc_title: Evaluation of certain food additives: one-hundredth report of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (WHO Technical Report Series 1058)
publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 1. Introduction
text:
Dr Sanaa welcomed all attendees to the meeting on behalf of WHO, and highlighted that the milestone of the One-hundredth JECFA meeting represents more than half a century of rigorous science, global collaboration and an unwavering commitment to public health. JECFA, formed in 1956 by just a few experts with the ambitious idea that food safety should be grounded in independent and evidence-based science, is today at the heart of the Joint FAO/ WHO Programme on Food Safety. This programme is one of the longest-running and most trusted scientific advisory mechanisms in the world, combining the technical strengths of FAO and WHO, the wisdom of the expert community and the ongoing support of Member States.

Dr Sanaa expressed gratitude to all the experts, both past and present, for their unwavering dedication, precious time spent analysing toxicological data, and commitment to independence and excellence. The contributions of these experts have established the credibility of JECFA. He also extended his thanks to the governments of the Member States for their trust, nominations, and financial and political support, essential for the continuation of this programme.

- 1 A full list of JECFA publications is provided as Annex 1.

doc_title: Evaluation of certain food additives: one-hundredth report of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (WHO Technical Report Series 1058)
publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 1. Introduction
text: Dr Sanaa highlighted that the meeting coincided with World Food Safety Day, which has the 2025 theme of “Food Safety: Science in Action”. He emphasized that JECFA embodies this theme, translating science into action through Codex standards and national regulations to improve the lives of global populations. He further stressed that reaching the One-hundredth meeting does not mean that JECFA can stop striving for progress; food systems are evolving, new hazards are emerging and science itself is transforming. To continue to make progress, JECFA must continue to attract new experts, integrate new methodologies such as in vitro tools and in silico models, and ensure that the Joint FAO/WHO Programme has the required resources. Dr Sanaa concluded that the One-hundredth JECFA meeting is not just a celebration of the past but a call to action: future JECFA committees must work together to build on this legacy, scale up ambitions and deliver the science that the world needs.

doc_title: Evaluation of certain food additives: one-hundredth report of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (WHO Technical Report Series 1058)
publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 2. General considerations
2.1 Requests from Codex Alimentarius for safety assessment
section_heading: 2.1 Requests from Codex Alimentarius for safety assessment
text: The Committee noted that to complete an evaluation of the safety of a chemical in food, information to characterize the hazard and estimate the dietary exposure needs to be available. In some cases, requests from Codex to the Committee to consider only dietary exposure to a food chemical have resulted in the Committee noting that the previous toxicological assessment and specifications are old and may not reflect current scientific knowledge, including the availability of new studies. The Committee therefore considers that requests from Codex should include a consideration of the toxicological data, including any new data available since the previous assessment, and information on chemical and technical considerations as well as dietary exposure necessary to conduct a full safety evaluation.

section_path: 2. General considerations
2.2 Mapping food categories of the General Standard for Food Additives (GSFA) to the FoodEx2 classifications
section_heading: 2.2 Mapping food categories of the General Standard for Food Additives (GSFA) to the FoodEx2 classifications
text:
The Committee is aware of the work that has been undertaken by a group of members of the Codex Committee for Food Additives (CCFA) to map the food categories in the Codex General Standard for Food Additives (GSFA) to the FoodEx2 food classification system of the European Food Saftey Authority (EFSA) (1).

Such a mapping was requested by the Committee at its Eighty-ninth meeting to enable the dietary exposure assessment for sucrose esters of fatty acids (INS [International Numbering System for Food Additives] No. 473) and sucrose oligoesters, type I and type II (INS No. 473a) to be undertaken using the FAO/WHO chronic individual food consumption database (CIFOCOss) (which is classified according to FoodEx2) and use levels provided. The need for the mapping was also noted by the Committee at its Ninety-ninth meeting for the same reason for polyglycerol esters of fatty acids (INS No. 475).

The mapping was provided to the JECFA secretariat in January 2025 and was used at the current meeting for the dietary exposure assessment for adipic acid (INS No. 355) and dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate (INS No. 480).

doc_title: Evaluation of certain food additives: one-hundredth report of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (WHO Technical Report Series 1058)
publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 2. General considerations
2.2 Mapping food categories of the General Standard for Food Additives (GSFA) to the FoodEx2 classifications
section_heading: 2.2 Mapping food categories of the General Standard for Food Additives (GSFA) to the FoodEx2 classifications
text:
The mapping was provided to the JECFA secretariat in January 2025 and was used at the current meeting for the dietary exposure assessment for adipic acid (INS No. 355) and dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate (INS No. 480).

The Committee noted that the mapping was comprehensive and was presented in several different ways that made it easy to review and use. The Committee also noted that there are some FoodEx2 categories that have multiple GSFA food categories assigned. This is because of how the food consumption data are described in different contexts (e.g. reported by nutrition survey respondents, described in nutrition surveys or summarized for inclusion in the CIFOCOss database), and because similar foods that are described in different categorization systems will have more than one direct alignment. This is a positive aspect of the mapping, and allows the JECFA dietary exposure experts to determine the particular concentration from which GSFA category to use for the assessment based on the knowledge of use of the food additive. These assumptions or decisions may vary between different assessments or scenarios.

The mapping, together with submitted use level information for food additives, will enable dietary exposures to be estimated for a greater number of food additives in the future and for a broad range of countries. This will inevitably better support the CCFA by providing evidence and conclusions from the safety assessments of food additives for risk management purposes, and will assist in the establishment of its priority list of food additives for evaluation by the Committee.

doc_title: Evaluation of certain food additives: one-hundredth report of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (WHO Technical Report Series 1058)
publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 2. General considerations
2.2 Mapping food categories of the General Standard for Food Additives (GSFA) to the FoodEx2 classifications
section_heading: 2.2 Mapping food categories of the General Standard for Food Additives (GSFA) to the FoodEx2 classifications
text:
The mapping, together with submitted use level information for food additives, will enable dietary exposures to be estimated for a greater number of food additives in the future and for a broad range of countries. This will inevitably better support the CCFA by providing evidence and conclusions from the safety assessments of food additives for risk management purposes, and will assist in the establishment of its priority list of food additives for evaluation by the Committee.

The Committee concluded that this mapping was very useful and enabled the fast and efficient assignment of concentration data to food consumption data for a large number of foods to enable dietary exposure calculations to be undertaken within the timeframes for the meeting. The Committee noted that the mapping will enable consistent use for its assessments for future meetings. The Commitee also noted that the use of the CIFOCOss data for a dietary exposure assessment will be decided on a case-by-case basis, taking into consideration the availability of other exposure estimates from the sponsor or the literature, the food groups included and the availability of concentration data. The eventual choice of whether to use CIFOCOss and the mapping can be made by the exposure experts.

The Committee recommends that the mapping be publicly available to promote its consistent application internationally, including assisting coding of food consumption databases for submission to FAO/WHO for inclusion in the CIFOCOss database.

2.3 Completion of enzyme specifications
text:
At its Ninety-fifth meeting, the Committee was only able to assign temporary acceptable daily intakes (ADIs) and prepare tentative specifications for several enzyme preparations on the agenda (Table 2.1) because of deficiencies in the data packages (2).

The Committee at its Ninety-fifth meeting noted that “the details of the assays supplied included the use of an enzyme reference or calibrant, rather than a direct link to an original enzyme assay from which a meaningful unit definition could be derived” (2). According to the guidance document Environmental Health Criteria (EHC) 240 chapter 9.1.4.2 (3), each evaluation requires a definition of the unit of enzyme activity and a validated method to measure it directly. These requirements are stated in items 21 and 22 in the checklist found in the appendix to the chapter, and were reproduced as annex 3, table A3.1 of the report of the Ninety-ninth meeting of the Committee (4).

doc_title: Evaluation of certain food additives: one-hundredth report of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (WHO Technical Report Series 1058)
publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 2. General considerations
2.4 Limits for lead in specifications of food additives for use in infant formula
section_heading: 2.4 Limits for lead in specifications of food additives for use in infant formula
text: The Committee at the present meeting considered three additives for use in infant formula and formula for special medical purposes (FSMP) for infants, namely ascorbyl palmitate, carob bean gum and gellan gum. The Committee noted that the Eighth session of the Codex Committee on Contaminants in Foods (5) set a maximum level of 0.01 mg/kg for lead in infant formula (as consumed). The Committee also noted that the use of two of the three additives (gellan gum and carob bean gum) at proposed use levels could result in an exceedance of the maximum level for lead in infant formula, if lead were present at the specified limit (i.e. 2 mg/kg in carob bean gum and gellan gum). The Committee noted that lower lead limits in the specifications (e.g. 0.5 mg/kg for carob bean gum and 0.5 mg/kg for gellan gum) would result in neither of the additives exceeding the maximum level for lead in the final infant formula (i.e. 0.01 mg/kg). This was calculated without considering the contribution of other ingredients to the overall lead level in infant formula. The Committee reaffirmed that the responsibility for ensuring that the final infant formula (as consumed) comply with the maximum level for lead remains with infant formula producers.

section_path: 2. General considerations
2.4 Limits for lead in specifications of food additives for use in infant formula
section_heading: 2.4 Limits for lead in specifications of food additives for use in infant formula
text:
Since these food additives are also used in the manufacture of other foods as well as infant formula, lower lead limits should be introduced in the specifications for additives used in infant formula. Specifications monographs already exist for carob bean gum and carob bean gum (clarified). A lower lead limit for infant formula was not added, despite agreement by the Committee at its Eighty-second meeting to do so, and is included in the errata (Chapter 4) considered at the present meeting. The Committee noted that data provided at the present meeting by the sponsors indicate that individual food additives can be produced with lead levels below the specified limits, as listed above. A new specifications monograph for low-acyl clarified gellan gum for applications in infant formula was developed at the current meeting, including a limit of

- 0.5 mg/kg for lead.

publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)
3.1 Toxicological and/or dietary exposure assessment, and specifications
3.1.1 Adipates
text:
Explanation

Adipic acid (INS No. 355) is a food additive permitted in the Codex GSFA as an acidity regulator. Adipic acid is also used as a flavouring agent.

At its Twenty-first meeting in 1977, the Committee reaffirmed an ADI for adipic acid of 0–5 mg/kg body weight (bw) (1), based on a reduced body weight gain in a long-term rat study that had been established at its Ninth meeting in 1965 (2). Details of the toxicological studies that supported the establishment of a group ADI of 0–5 mg/kg bw for adipic acid and its potassium (INS No. 357), sodium (INS No. 356) and ammonium (INS No. 359) salts were made available in the monograph of the Twenty-first meeting (3). Adipic acid was also evaluated by the Committee at its Fifty-third meeting in 1999 as a flavouring agent, when it was concluded that there were no safety concerns with current levels of exposure for this use (4).

At the Forty-eighth session of the CCFA (5), it was noted during the process of proposing provisions for adipic acid for the GSFA that the Committee had not undertaken a dietary exposure assessment. A circular letter was issued to Codex members and observers to request the submission of use level information for adipic acid to enable a dietary exposure assessment to be conducted (6).

A literature search was undertaken to identify any publications including estimates of dietary exposure to, or use levels of, adipic acid. No publications were identified.

Assessment of dietary exposure

The Committee evaluated information on use levels provided in response to the Codex circular letter and submitted to the Committee for consideration, and dietary exposure estimates submitted to and calculated by the Committee.

The dietary exposure was assessed based on three scenarios of concentration levels: (i) GSFA current maximum levels (for three food categories);

(ii) GSFA current and proposed maximum levels (three current [one with a higher proposed maximum level] and 19 additional food categories); and (iii) use levels (36 food categories). The FAO/WHO CIFOCOss food consumption dataset was used to calculate estimates of dietary exposure. The FoodEx2 to GSFA food category mapping provided to the JECFA secretariat in 2025 was used to assign concentrations to food categories consumed. The range of estimated dietary exposures for each of the concentration scenarios for children and adults is provided in Table 3.1. Estimated dietary exposures range between less than 0.001 and 410 mg/kg bw per day across all the mean and high estimates for all child and adult population subgroups and concentration scenarios assessed. The main contributors to dietary exposure were assessed as individual foods that resulted in dietary exposures of more than 5 mg/kg bw per day. For the GSFA current maximum levels scenario, these were flavoured milks and yoghurts for children only. For the GSFA current and proposed maximum levels scenario, these were confectionery, desserts, sauces, beverages and yoghurts for both children and adults. doc_title: Evaluation of certain food additives: one-hundredth report of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (WHO Technical Report Series 1058)
publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)
3.1 Toxicological and/or dietary exposure assessment, and specifications
3.1.1 Adipates
text:
The Committee noted that the estimates of dietary exposure calculated at the current meeting are overestimated for a number of reasons, including: the large number of food categories included; the magnitude of the concentrations; the assumption of maximum permitted levels, or the upper end of the range of reported use levels in the food categories; and the assumption that all foods that could contain adipic acid do contain this food additive.

The Committee concluded that most of these conservative dietary exposure estimates greatly exceed the current group ADI of 0–5 mg/kg bw. For the GSFA current maximum levels scenario, for children there was exceedance of the group ADI by up to 660% for high exposures. For the GSFA current and proposed maximum levels scenario, the group ADI was exceeded for children and adults by up to around 8000% for high exposures and for the use levels scenario by up to 3000% for high exposures.

Further, the Committee noted that there is the potential for exceedances of the current group ADI as a result of normal daily consumption amounts of an individual food. For example, using the current permitted maximum level for flavoured milks of 1500 mg/kg, children only need to consume 67 g/day and adults 200 g/day before the group ADI is exceeded. For food containing adipic acid at the proposed maximum level for the GSFA of 50 000 mg/kg, consumption of only a few grams would result in an exceedance of the current group ADI. Many of the foods with use levels that would result in exceedance of the group ADI are frequently or daily consumed foods.

The Committee noted that hazard assessment procedures have evolved and additional relevant data may have become available since the numerical ADI was established at its Ninth meeting in 1965, indicating that a re-evaluation of the toxicology of adipic acid is needed.

An addendum to the dietary exposure monograph was prepared.

Recommendations

Recommendations

The Committee requests submission of any updated or additional data on use levels of adipic acid to refine the estimates of dietary exposure, including:

- minimum use levels that achieve the technological function of the additive in the range of relevant foods;
- any further or more specific information on typical use levels;
- updated information on proposed maximum levels;
- an updated list of food categories for which uses are actually required; and
- national estimates of dietary exposure based on individual dietary records and typical use levels. The Committee recommends that an updated toxicological evaluation,

including the reassessment of the current group ADI, be conducted.

Updated assessments of toxicological data, dietary exposure estimates and specifications would allow a full safety assessment for this food additive to be completed by the Committee.

The safety evaluation could not be completed at the Ninety-fifth meeting because of the tentative nature of the specifications and the inability to complete the allergenicity assessment. text:
Chemical and technical considerations

In the data submitted for the Ninety-fifth meeting for the evaluation of this enzyme, the activity was expressed in amyloglucosidase units (AGU) per gram relative to a proprietary enzyme standard. The mean activity of amyloglucosidase from four batches of the enzyme concentrate was 400 AGU/g (corresponding to

- 4.2 AGU/mg TOS). In the data submitted to the current meeting, enzyme activity was expressed in glucoamylase M units per gram as described in the specifications monograph for amyloglucosidase from R. emersonii expressed in A. niger. One glucoamylase M unit is defined as the amount of enzyme required to liberate
- 0.1 mmol/min of p-nitrophenol (PNP) from p-nitrophenyl-α-d-glucopyranoside (PNPG) solution under the conditions of the assay (pH 4.3, 50 °C). The mean activity of amyloglucosidase from five batches of enzyme concentrate was 498.2 glucoamylase M units/g (equivalent to 425.2 AGU/g). The conversion factor from AGU/g to glucoamylase M units/g is about 1.2. The mean TOS of the five batches of enzyme concentrate was 10.3% and the mean enzyme activity/TOS ratio was 4.9 glucoamylase M units/mg TOS. This amyloglucosidase enzyme preparation is used at a maximum level of 931 mg TOS/kg starch-based raw material for solid foods and 1090 mg TOS/kg starch-based raw material for non-milk beverages (9).

text:
Assessment of potential allergenicity

The Committee previously evaluated the potential for allergenicity of the enzyme preparation (9) by conducting a homology search of the amino acid sequence of amyloglucosidase with those of known allergens in the AllergenOnline (14)

and Allergen (15) databases, according to bioinformatics criteria recommended by EHC 240 (13). The previous Committee identified a match to a respiratory allergen, the amyloglucosidase Sch c 1 found in split-gill mushrooms (Schizophyllum commune) that is associated with occupational asthma in bakers (16–18). This allergen showed 60–84% identity with amyloglucosidase over a sliding window of 80 amino acids (with and without scaling); 47.9% identity over the full length of the protein; and 10 matches based on a 100% identity over eight contiguous amino acids. The previous Committee acknowledged that amyloglucosidase could pose a risk as a respiratory allergen that, when ingested, may also cause a food allergy (17,18). However, the previous Committee also noted that S. commune is consumed as a traditional food throughout Asia and Central America, and there are no published reports of S. commune being linked to a food allergen. - 9 mg TOS/kg bw per day yields a margin of exposure (MOE) of more than 160. Explanation

Ascorbyl palmitate (INS No. 304) is a food additive used as an antioxidant in a wide range of foods and beverages, including infant formula, FSMP for infants and food for young children.

At its Forty-third session, the Codex Committee on Nutrition and Foods for Special Dietary Uses (CCNFSDU) (20) concluded that the use of ascorbyl palmitate as an antioxidant at 1 mg/100 mL in all types of formula covered by food category (FC) 13.1.1 Infant formulae was technologically justified. section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)

3.1.3 Ascorbyl palmitate
text:
Chemical and technical considerations

Ascorbyl palmitate (CAS No. 137-66-6) is an ester formed from the reaction of the primary alcohol group of ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and the carboxylic group of palmitic acid. Its chemical formula is C22H38O7 and its molecular weight is 414.5 g/mol. Ascorbyl palmitate can be produced enzymatically or by chemical synthesis. Chemical synthesis of ascorbyl palmitate involves esterification in the presence of sulfuric acid, followed by extraction with suitable solvents (petroleum ether, mesityl oxide and acetone) and further purification steps. The final product, a white or yellow-white powder with a citrus-like odour, is 98% pure on the dried basis.

Ascorbyl palmitate functions as an antioxidant, providing a fat-soluble alternative to ascorbic acid. It is used in various food categories, including infant formula, follow-up formula and formula intended for special medical purposes for infants.

When stored in the dark under ambient conditions, ascorbyl palmitate is stable for at least 30 months. The oxidation mechanism of ascorbyl palmitate in food is expected to be that of ascorbic acid. The fate of ascorbyl palmitate in food is expected to be similar to that of ascorbic acid and palmitic acid.

Biochemical aspects

Ascorbyl palmitate, an ester of ascorbic acid and palmitic acid, is extensively hydrolysed in the gastrointestinal tract to its constituent acids (26–29).

publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)
3.1 Toxicological and/or dietary exposure assessment, and specifications
3.1.3 Ascorbyl palmitate
text:
Ascorbyl palmitate, an ester of ascorbic acid and palmitic acid, is extensively hydrolysed in the gastrointestinal tract to its constituent acids (26–29).

Hydrolysis is mediated by carboxylesterases, mainly carboxylesterase-2, present in the gastrointestinal tract (30–33). Although expression of carboxylesterases is lower in infants (age < 1 year) than in adults, the esterase is present in the neonatal liver and duodenum, and expression levels increase rapidly in infants during postnatal development (34–38).

Rapid and extensive hydrolysis of ascorbyl palmitate (0.1 and 0.2 mM, equivalent to gastrointestinal concentrations of approximately 40 and 80 mg/L, respectively) into ascorbic acid and palmitic acid was observed in a more recent in vitro study with simulated intestinal fluid containing bile acids and pancreatic enzymes (29).

Increased concentrations of ascorbic acid were observed in plasma, liver, spleen, adrenals and brain following oral administration of ascorbic acid or ascorbyl palmitate to guinea pigs (27,28). Increased urinary excretion of ascorbic acid was observed following intake of ascorbyl palmitate (700 mg or 4.7 g per day) by human volunteers (26,28).

The Committee concluded that any ascorbyl palmitate that was not hydrolysed in the gastrointestinal tract would be subject to hydrolysis to ascorbic acid and palmitic acid in the liver. Ascorbic acid and palmitic acid are normal components of the human diet and undergo typical metabolic pathways following absorption.

publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)
3.1 Toxicological and/or dietary exposure assessment, and specifications
3.1.3 Ascorbyl palmitate
text:
Toxicological studies

In a study previously evaluated by the Committee, no adverse effects were observed in rats fed ascorbyl palmitate for 2 years at 125 mg/kg bw per day, the highest dose tested (22,23).

Ascorbyl palmitate was not mutagenic in a bacterial reverse mutation assay at concentrations up to 3.3 mg per plate (39). Although genotoxicity studies examining the full range of end-points were not available, the Committee noted that ascorbyl palmitate is metabolized in the gastrointestinal tract to ascorbic and palmitic acid, which does not raise any concerns for genotoxicity.

Dietary administration of ascorbyl palmitate to mice and rats did not show a promoting effect on azoxymethanol- or azoxymethane-induced colon tumours (40,41).

Observations in humans

No adverse effects were associated with the consumption of bread fortified with ascorbyl palmitate at concentrations of up to 890 mg/100 g in a self-controlled, 28-day study in women aged 35–45 years (42).

In seven paediatric trials, no adverse effects attributable to feeding with infant formula containing ascorbyl palmitate were found (43–49). However, the concentrations of ascorbyl palmitate in the infant formula tested were not given; these studies were therefore not useful to the assessment of the safety of ascorbyl palmitate in infants.

No adverse events have been reported in post-market surveillance data representative of over 175 million consumption days of infant formula containing ascorbyl palmitate at levels of 100 mg/L (as consumed).

publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)

3.1.3 Ascorbyl palmitate
text:
Assessment of dietary exposure

At its current meeting, the Committee evaluated the dietary exposure to ascorbyl palmitate based on the current and requested maximum levels in foods for infants aged up to 1 year (FC 13.1.1, 13.1.2 and 13.1.3) and dietetic foods for special medical purposes (FC 13.3). As the maximum levels refer to the products “as consumed”, they are provided in units of milligrams per litre (mg/L).

Dietary exposure was assessed using consumption data for infant and follow-up formula based on enteral feeding volumes for preterm infants (< 37 weeks gestation), WHO-recommended consumption levels, estimated energy requirements, actual reported levels and consumption levels of infant formula as proposed by the Scientific Committee of EFSA (50). Based on these consumption levels, dietary exposure to ascorbyl palmitate at current maximum levels of 10 or 50 mg/L ranged from 0.6 to 6.1 mg/kg bw per day, and at the requested maximum level of 100 mg/L ranged from 3.5 to 26 mg/kg bw per day.

For dietetic foods at the current maximum level of 10 mg/L, a high exposure of 0.9 mg/kg bw per day was calculated based on a high consumption of two servings of 330 g/day and an adult body weight of 70 kg. At the requested maximum level of 100 mg/L, the dietary exposure would increase to 9.4 mg/kg bw per day. These dietary exposure estimates are based on the expansion of the use of ascorbyl palmitate in FC 13.3 to include dietetic foods captured under this food category that can be consumed by population groups aged 5 years and older.

Based on these consumption levels, dietary exposure to ascorbyl palmitate at current maximum levels of 10 or 50 mg/L ranged from 0.6 to 6.1 mg/kg bw per day, and at the requested maximum level of 100 mg/L ranged from 3.5 to 26 mg/kg bw per day.

For dietetic foods at the current maximum level of 10 mg/L, a high exposure of 0.9 mg/kg bw per day was calculated based on a high consumption of two servings of 330 g/day and an adult body weight of 70 kg. At the requested maximum level of 100 mg/L, the dietary exposure would increase to 9.4 mg/kg bw per day. These dietary exposure estimates are based on the expansion of the use of ascorbyl palmitate in FC 13.3 to include dietetic foods captured under this food category that can be consumed by population groups aged 5 years and older.

text:
Evaluation

The Committee noted new studies that showed that ascorbyl palmitate was rapidly and extensively hydrolysed pre-systemically to ascorbic acid and palmitic acid. Hydrolysis of ascorbyl palmitate is mediated by carboxylesterases, which are also expressed in neonates and infants, albeit at lower levels than in adults. On that basis, the Committee considered that systemic exposure to ascorbyl palmitate would be low for all population subgroups.

The Committee further noted that ascorbic acid and palmitic acid are normal components of the human diet. A group ADI “not specified”6 has been established by previous Committees for ascorbic acid and its sodium, potassium and calcium salts, and a group ADI “not specified” has been established for palmitic acid and its sodium, potassium and calcium salts. The Committee therefore withdrew the previously established ADI of 0–1.25 mg/kg bw for ascorbyl palmitate or ascorbyl stearate, or the sum of both. The Committee noted that the previous ADI for ascorbyl palmitate or ascorbyl stearate, or the sum of both, was based on toxicological data for ascorbyl palmitate, and therefore established a group ADI “not specified” for ascorbyl palmitate or ascorbyl stearate, or the sum of both.

The requested increase of the maximum level from 10 to 100 mg/kg for ascorbyl palmitate in dietetic foods for special medical purposes (FC 13.3), and expansion of the use of ascorbyl palmitate in FC 13.3 to include all dietetic foods captured under this category, do not pose a concern for safety.

text:
At the present meeting the Committee only received information for chemically synthesized ascorbyl palmitate and prepared revised specifications accordingly. The Committee lowered the existing limit for lead, added specifications for arsenic and mercury, modified the method of assay to avoid the use of chloroform, increased the assay value from 95% to 98%, and added specifications for residual solvents (acetone, petroleum ether and mesityl oxide) and a method for their determination.

The Committee discussed lead specifications for ascorbyl palmitate and the other food additives considered for use in infant formula that were on the agenda, as described in Section 2.4. The current specification for ascorbyl palmitate restricts the level of lead to not more than 1 mg/kg. Considering the newly proposed maximum use level for ascorbyl palmitate in infant formula of 100 mg/L as consumed, and the maximum permissible level of lead in ascorbyl palmitate, the contribution of lead from ascorbyl palmitate in infant formula is expected to be less than 0.0001 mg/L.

An addendum to the toxicological and dietary exposure monograph was prepared.

The specifications monograph and chemical and technical assessment were revised.

Recommendations

The Committee noted that ascorbyl stearate specifications need analogous revision and recommended that the additive be included in a future call for data.

At its Eighty-second meeting in 2017 the Committee concluded that the studies available were not sufficient for the evaluation of carob bean gum for use in infant formula (55). The Committee requested toxicological data from studies in neonatal animals, adequate to evaluate the safety for use in infant formula, to complete the evaluation. At the Eighty-second meeting the Committee also conducted a dietary exposure assessment for the use of carob bean gum in infant formula for infants younger than 12 weeks (55). At a proposed maximum use level of 10 000 mg/L and a number of consumption scenarios, estimates of dietary exposure ranged from 600 to 1800 mg/kg bw per day and up to 2100 mg/kg bw per day for infants with high energy intakes.

An overview of clinical studies conducted with carob bean gum and three publications were also provided. A literature search was conducted by the Committee to retrieve information on carob bean gum toxicity published since 2016 (latest JECFA evaluation). This literature search identified four relevant publications not previously considered.

No new information on chemical and technical considerations was submitted.

text:
Biochemical aspects

No new information on absorption, distribution, metabolism or elimination of carob bean gum was available. During its previous evaluation, the Committee concluded that carob bean gum is largely non-digestible and not bioavailable. Carob bean gum is fermented by microbiota in the gut, producing oligosaccharides or monosaccharides that are converted to short-chain fatty acids. These short-chain fatty acids can then be absorbed and metabolized in normal biochemical pathways.

Toxicological studies

In its previous evaluation, the Committee considered carob bean gum used as a food additive to be a substance of low oral toxicity. Carob bean gum was not carcinogenic or mutagenic, and not associated with any reproductive or developmental toxicity (55). The NOAEL identified for carob bean gum in 13-week studies ranged from 2500 to 10 000 mg/kg bw per day in rats and from 7500 to 15 000 mg/kg bw per day in mice, the highest doses tested. During its Twenty-fourth meeting in 1980 the Committee established an ADI “not specified” for carob bean gum (53).

One new in vitro study with metabolically competent human cell lines LS-174T (colon) and HepG2 (liver), as well as human cell lines ACHN (kidney) and SH-SY5Y (neuron) without metabolic capacity, confirmed that carob bean gum lacks genotoxic activity under the conditions of the study (56).

However, the Committee concluded that results from the pig study were not sufficient for the evaluation of carob bean gum for use in infant formula since the animal model used did not mimic the infant gut over the 12-week developmental period. In response to the reservations highlighted in the Committee’s previous evaluation (55), a new unpublished study (57) with carob bean gum administered in a piglet-adapted formula to neonatal Göttingen minipigs fed for 21 days from postnatal day (PND) 7 or 8, dosed with 0, 1.05, 1.50 or 2.40 g carob bean gum/ kg bw per day on average, was made available to the present Committee. The only effects observed related to carob bean gum were (i) a statistically significant decrease in serum zinc concentrations in high-dose males and in mid- and high-dose females; and (ii) dose-related increases in serum glucose levels in mid- and high-dose females. During its previous evaluation, the Committee described results from studies that measured the potential of carob bean gum to decrease the bioavailability of minerals. Those studies suggested that infant formula with a carob bean gum concentration of more than 4 g/L reduced the levels of calcium, zinc and iron available for absorption; however, that effect was not considered to be unique to carob bean gum because it was also observed with other fibres such as oligofructose, maltodextrin and high-esterified pectin. Additionally, the previous Committee described an open randomized prospective study in healthy infants addressing the bioavailability of intestinal minerals and other nutrients with commercially available infant formula containing 4 g/L carob bean gum. Mean zinc levels were not statistically significantly different between treated and control groups.

The Committee also noted that the piglets were not fasted before sampling the blood, and that the blood glucose levels reported for both treated and control groups in this new study were, according to the authors, higher than historical control data in fasted piglets. The Committee also noted that the piglets were not fasted before sampling the blood, and that the blood glucose levels reported for both treated and control groups in this new study were, according to the authors, higher than historical control data in fasted piglets. The Committee further noted that carob bean gum comprises galactose and mannose subunits (59) and therefore that the two sugar moieties will be released by fermentation of carob bean gum by microbiota (60). Galactose and mannose will interfere with the quantitative determination of glucose, leading to an overestimation of plasma glucose levels. The Committee therefore concluded that the dose-related increase in apparent glucose levels was likely to be related to the release of galactose and mannose from carob bean gum, and is not an adverse effect. The Committee identified a NOAEL of 2.40 g/kg bw per day carob bean gum, the highest dose tested, as part of a thickened infant formula from the 21-day study of neonatal minipigs fed a piglet-adapted formula.

publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)
3.1 Toxicological and/or dietary exposure assessment, and specifications
3.1.4 Carob bean gum
text:
Observations in humans

In its previous evaluation the Committee concluded that the prevalence of oral hypersensitivity to carob bean gum in the overall population is expected to be very low and not of concern. During that evaluation, the Committee considered

- 13 paediatric tolerance trials conducted with infant formula containing carob bean gum as a thickening agent. No adverse events were reported in any of the studies, which included about 400 term infants fed formula from the age of 1 week to 3 months containing carob bean gum concentrations ranging from 3500 to 6000 mg/L. Those studies measured the effects of carob bean gum formula on regurgitation frequencies in infants with uncomplicated gastro-oesophageal reflux, growth, formula intake, and volume and characteristics of stool. Although those trials were of limited duration and were specifically designed to measure the effects of thickened formula on the treatment of gastro-oesophageal reflux, they demonstrate tolerance of infants exposed to carob bean gum.

Three new publications on paediatric trials were made available to the Committee (61–63). Those publications tested tolerance to an infant formula containing 4000 mg/L carob bean gum as a thickener in infants with uncomplicated regurgitation. Except for an increased incidence of sporadic flatulence, soft stools, constipation and abdominal pain in the test group, no other adverse events were reported in infants after 3 months of feeding for the longest trials. Regurgitation frequency was reduced in infants fed the formula thickened with carob bean gum compared with control infants.

3.1.4 Carob bean gum
text:
Microbiological studies

The faecal microbiota composition was analysed from piglet stool samples obtained in the previously described study (57) with neonatal Göttingen minipigs fed a piglet-adapted formula containing carob bean gum for 21 days from PND 7 or 8 (64). Control piglets were fed a non-thickened formula. No response related to carob bean gum could be identified among the targeted bacterial groups under the conditions of the study.

Assessment of dietary exposure

The Committee assessed the dietary exposure to carob bean gum from infant formula.

For the purpose of the evaluation, the Committee used the highest consumption data available for infant formula of 200 and 260 g/kg bw per day for an average and high consumer, respectively, and dietary exposure estimates based on three concentration scenarios. (i) Carob bean gum is permitted for use in infant formula products in the GSFA at a maximum level of 1000 mg/L (as consumed) (65). The level of 1000 mg/L carob bean gum in infant formula leads to dietary exposures estimated by the Committee of 200 mg/kg bw per day (average consumer) and 260 mg/kg bw per day (high consumer) for infants.

(ii) The upper end of the range of use levels of 6000 mg/L carob bean gum in infant formula from paediatric trials leads to dietary exposures estimated by the Committee of 1200 mg/kg bw per day (average consumer) and 1560 mg/kg bw per day (high consumer) for infants. (iii) The maximum use level of 10 000 mg/L provided by the sponsor that was used by the Eighty-second Committee resulted in estimates of dietary exposure to carob bean gum of 2000 mg/kg bw per day (average consumer) and 2600 mg/kg bw per day (high consumer) for infants.

text:
Evaluation

The Committee previously assigned an ADI “not specified”8 to carob bean gum. However, an ADI does not apply to infants younger than 12 weeks since they might be at risk at lower levels of exposure compared with older age groups. To complete the evaluation, the Committee therefore requested studies in neonatal animals adequate for the evaluation of the safety of carob bean gum in infant formula.

Newly submitted unpublished data obtained from a neonatal pig study evaluated at the present meeting allowed the Committee to identify a NOAEL of 2400 mg/kg bw per day, the highest dose tested.

Based on the estimated high dietary exposures for infants, the Committee noted that MOEs calculated for the use of carob bean gum at 1000 mg/L and 6000 mg/L in infant formula were 9 and 1.5, respectively. The MOE for the high exposure calculated for infants from the use of carob bean gum at 10 000 mg/L in infant formula was less than 1.

To interpret an MOE related to exposure in infants, the Committee has previously established several considerations that need to be addressed (66). If these considerations are met, MOEs in the region of 1–10 may indicate low risk for the health of infants aged 0–12 weeks exposed to the food additive through infant formula (66). The considerations relevant for the current evaluation are:

doc_title: Evaluation of certain food additives: one-hundredth report of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (WHO Technical Report Series 1058)
publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)
3.1 Toxicological and/or dietary exposure assessment, and specifications
3.1.4 Carob bean gum
text:
To interpret an MOE related to exposure in infants, the Committee has previously established several considerations that need to be addressed (66). If these considerations are met, MOEs in the region of 1–10 may indicate low risk for the health of infants aged 0–12 weeks exposed to the food additive through infant formula (66). The considerations relevant for the current evaluation are:

(i) no adverse effects were observed in any of the studies available, indicating that the toxicity of carob bean gum is low; (ii) the NOAEL was the highest dose tested in a study in neonatal pigs considered as a relevant animal model for human infants; (iii) a number of paediatric trials of infant formula containing carob bean gum show good tolerance of infants to carob bean gum at concentrations of up to 6000 mg/L (0.6%); (iv) the prevalence of hypersensitivity to carob bean gum orally is expected to be very low; (v) the highest exposure estimates consider high intake scenarios; and (vi) the duration of the exposure will be short and followed by diversification in the diet of the infants. Furthermore, the Committee observed that there is a variety of medical conditions among infants requiring FSMP, and that those infants would normally be under medical supervision. The Committee concluded that the MOEs based on carob bean gum concentrations of 1000 and 6000 mg/L in infant formula indicate a low risk; however, the MOE based on a concentration of 10 000 mg/L indicates a potential risk. Based on the available data and considering the short exposure period involved, the Committee concluded that there is no concern for the disruption of the intestinal microbiota by carob bean gum used as a thickener in infant formula.

3.1.5 Dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate
text:
Explanation

Dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate (DSS) (INS No. 480) is permitted for use in FC 04.1.2.9 Fruit-based desserts, including fruit-flavoured water-based desserts at a maximum level of 15 mg/kg, as specified in the GSFA. DSS was on the agenda of the present meeting of the Committee as requested at the Fifty-fourth session of the CCFA (21). Only an evaluation of the dietary exposure was requested. Dietary exposure to DSS as a food additive has not previously been evaluated by the Committee.

A temporary ADI for DSS of 0–0.25 mg/kg bw per day was established by the Committee at its Thirty-seventh meeting in 1990, based on a NOAEL of

- 50 mg/kg bw per day from a reproductive toxicity study in rats and an uncertainty factor9 of 200 (68). The adverse effect was a reduction in parental body weight and weanling pup weight. The ADI was temporary, “pending the evaluation, in 1995, of the results of the long-term study in a rodent species that was requested earlier”. However, at its Forty-fourth meeting in 1995, no such data were available to the Committee (69). Because of this, the Forty-fourth Committee concluded that “dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate could be evaluated on the basis of the limited data available because of a low intake anticipated”. The Committee withdrew its request for a long-term study and increased the uncertainty factor to 500 because of the limited toxicological database, resulting in an ADI of 0–0.1 mg/kg bw per day. The Committee also conducted a literature search to consider any studies on dietary exposure to DSS. No studies were identified for inclusion in the evaluation.

Assessment of dietary exposure

text:
FC: food category; GSFA: General Standard for Food Additives.

The Committee evaluated the submitted estimates of dietary exposure to DSS based on the use levels and individual food consumption data from the United Kingdom and the USA. Additionally, the Committee calculated the dietary exposure to DSS by mapping the use levels to individual food consumption data from 47 dietary surveys in 22 European countries using the DietEx Exposure tool (70). The estimates were either calculated with the maximum use levels and presented as the maximum exposure scenario, or calculated with a combination of maximum and average use levels (presented as the refined exposure scenario). In the refined exposure scenario, the consumption of fruit-flavoured soft drinks within the two types of soft drinks was mapped to the maximum use levels, and the consumption of non-fruit-flavoured soft drinks was mapped to the average use levels. This scenario was based on information from the industry that DSS is only used in fruit-flavoured soft drinks. As the estimates of the two scenarios were similar, a summary of the estimates according to the refined exposure scenario is provided in Table 3.3. The estimates were similar because the exposure to DSS at the upper end of the exposure estimate ranges was largely determined by fruit-flavoured soft drinks. Furthermore, the Committee noted that the use of DSS in soft drinks is not permitted in the United Kingdom or in the European Union (EU). The estimates for the United Kingdom and the EU therefore represent potential high estimate exposure scenarios, considering the consumption of soft drinks in these countries.

3.1.5 Dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate
text:
At its Forty-fourth meeting in 1995, the Committee established an ADI of 0–0.1 mg/kg bw for DSS (69). The high (P95) dietary exposure estimates of DSS of up to 0.30 mg/kg bw per day for children aged 1–17 years could exceed this ADI. The estimates for adults were all below the ADI.

Considering that (i) the dietary exposure estimates are conservative because of the assumptions that all soft drinks that could contain DSS do contain this food additive (although other food additives that perform the same function in foods are available) and, when DSS is used, it will always be present at the maximum and/or average use levels; and (ii) the ranges of exposure estimates based on only maximum use levels were comparable to those based on a combination of maximum and average use levels, the Committee concluded that the use of DSS as a food additive in soft drinks and fruit-flavoured water-based desserts does not pose a safety concern.

A dietary exposure monograph was prepared.

Recommendations

The Committee noted that any further increases in exposure to DSS, for example as a result of higher use levels or an extension of its use in other food categories, would warrant an updated toxicological evaluation, including a reassessment of the current ADI (which was established 30 years ago).

section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)

3.1.6 Gardenia (Genipin) Blue
text:
Explanation

At the request of the CCFA at its Fifty-third session (71), the Committee evaluated the safety of Gardenia (Genipin) Blue (INS No. 165). Gardenia (Genipin) Blue is a water-soluble, dark purple to blue powder used as a colourant.

Gardenia (Genipin) Blue is intended to impart blue or green colour to different food types, including specific alcoholic beverages; sport and energy drinks; flavoured water; fruit drinks; carbonated soft drinks; powdered beverages; jams, jellies and marmalades; chewing gum; ready-to-drink teas; sugar coatings; icings; syrups for shaved ice; ice cream and frozen dairy desserts; hard and soft candy; flavoured milk; yogurt; processed cereals; sponge cakes; and food supplements (e.g. chewable tablets). Gardenia (Genipin) Blue is approved for use in foods in China; Taiwan, China; Japan; and the Republic of Korea.

The Committee has not previously evaluated the safety of Gardenia (Genipin) Blue. However, at its Eighty-fourth meeting, a previous Committee considered Gardenia Blue to be structurally related to Jagua (Genipin Glycine) Blue and evaluated data from a 104-week oral toxicity study on a Gardenia Blue polymer (72) to evaluate the safety of Jagua (Genipin Glycine) Blue (73). The Committee did not identify any treatment-related adverse effects in that study, but noted that it was a non-GLP study that did not describe the purity and content of the Gardenia Blue polymer in the test material.

doc_title: Evaluation of certain food additives: one-hundredth report of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (WHO Technical Report Series 1058)
publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)
3.1 Toxicological and/or dietary exposure assessment, and specifications
3.1.6 Gardenia (Genipin) Blue
text:
The sponsor submitted a dossier containing chemical, technical, dietary exposure and toxicological data, including unpublished reports of several studies conducted with Gardenia (Genipin) Blue. These studies evaluated the biochemical aspects and different toxicological end-points, including short- and long-term oral toxicity, genotoxicity, and reproductive and developmental toxicity of Gardenia (Genipin) Blue. At the request of the Committee, the sponsor also submitted reports of six genotoxicity studies conducted with genipin.

The Committee evaluated the submitted data and conducted a literature search on Gardenia Blue that identified eight publications considered relevant to the present evaluation. The Committee also conducted a literature search to locate relevant toxicological data on two potential impurities in Gardenia (Genipin) Blue, geniposide and genipin, and identified 11 publications considered relevant to the current evaluation.

Chemical and technical considerations

Gardenia jasminoides Ellis is an evergreen shrub belonging to the Rubiaceae family (74). It grows to a height of 2–3 m and produces dark green shiny leaves and white fragrant flowers. It is native to Asia and mainly grows in tropical and subtropical regions. The fruits are used in the production of yellow, blue, red and green pigments widely used as food colouring materials in Japan and East Asia (75). They have also been used in traditional Chinese medicines for centuries (76). The dried fruits are referred to as Zhizi Guo in China, Sanshishi in Japan and Cape Jasmine in the Republic of Korea.

text: Gardenia fruits are rich in iridoid glycosides, which are the primary bioactive constituents of the fruit (74). Iridoids are secondary plant metabolites and represent the largest group of monoterpenoids with a cyclopentane-[C]-pyran skeleton (77,78). Iridoids can be non-glycosylated or glycosylated (78). Approximately 48 iridoid glycosides from Gardenia fruit have been identified and characterized, with geniposide being the most abundant (75,79).

publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)
3.1 Toxicological and/or dietary exposure assessment, and specifications
3.1.6 Gardenia (Genipin) Blue
text: The starting material is ripe, dried and crushed Gardenia fruit, which is extracted with water or ethanol. The extract is filtered to remove the yellow pigments crocin and crocetin. The colourless geniposide in the filtrate is enzymatically hydrolysed by β-glucosidase to the genipin aglycone (75,76,78,80). This reaction is carried out under specific conditions of pH, temperature, time and enzyme-substrate ratio. Upon completion of the reaction, the solution containing genipin is heated to inactivate the β-glucosidase and cooled. Soy protein hydrolysate is added to this reaction mixture in the presence of oxygen to form the characteristic dark purple to blue polymer (75,81). The product is further refined through successive filtration steps to remove insoluble substances and low-molecular-weight precursors (e.g. genipin and geniposide). Food-grade dextrin or maltodextrin are added to the liquid concentrate and spray-dried to give a powdered product. Batches of Gardenia (Genipin) Blue are manufactured in accordance with GMP, resulting in an article of commerce with a colour value of 300 and consisting of the Gardenia Blue polymer (28.5–36.3%), maltodextrin and/or dextrin (55.6–61.1%), and water (4.1–6.6%).

text:
The chemical formula for the Gardenia Blue polymer is (C11H7NO2R)n where n ≥ 4, and its structural formula is depicted in Fig. 3.1. The Gardenia Blue polymer is composed of genipin moieties containing peptide chains (81). The genipin moieties are linked via an alkene bridge. It has been quantified and characterized by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (13C) (81). The Gardenia Blue polymer has a molecular weight of 15 000–30 000 Da.

Geniposide and genipin, as potential impurities, are specified at no more than 80 and 5 mg/kg, respectively.

Gardenia (Genipin) Blue is stable for at least 63 months under storage conditions (1–10 °C) in a laminated bag.

Biochemical aspects

The Committee evaluated data from single- and repeat-dose studies on absorption, distribution and elimination conducted with Gardenia (Genipin) Blue in rats and mice (82). The Committee noted that the test material used in these studies had a Gardenia Blue polymer content of 24.7%, which was representative of the article of commerce. The absorption, distribution and elimination studies indicated that the Gardenia Blue polymer was poorly absorbed (< 2%) upon oral exposure and about 97% of the administered dose was eliminated unchanged in the faeces. Up to 0.5% of the administered dose was eliminated in the urine. The Committee also noted that Gardenia Blue polymer did not accumulate in any of the evaluated tissues, including kidneys.

text: No animal studies on the metabolism of Gardenia (Genipin) Blue were available. The sponsor submitted an in vitro digestibility study conducted with Gardenia (Genipin) Blue in SGF at a pH of 1.2 that evaluated levels of geniposide and genipin in the presence or absence of pepsin (83). Geniposide was detected in the SGF in the absence or presence of pepsin, and the level of genipin was below the level of quantification (LOQ < 50 ng/g) in this experimental matrix. text:
The Committee also reviewed data from publications that reported the potential hydrolysis of geniposide into genipin at intestinal pH in the presence of β-d-glucosidase (84–86). The Committee therefore considered genipin also as a potential hydrolysis product of geniposide in the body. The Committee evaluated a study in rats (87) that assessed the levels of genipin and genipin sulfate in the plasma after single oral administration of 480 mg/kg or 980 mg/kg of geniposide present in Gardenia fruit decoction. The Committee noted that no geniposide or genipin was detected in the plasma throughout the study; however, genipin sulfate was detected, which was rapidly eliminated via urine. The Committee considered that, being highly reactive, genipin from the Gardenia fruit decoction rapidly conjugates with sulfate. There is therefore no systemic exposure to free genipin upon oral administration. The Committee concluded that if any geniposide from Gardenia (Genipin) Blue hydrolyses to genipin in the intestine, genipin would rapidly undergo sulfate conjugation pre-systemically and then be eliminated completely as genipin sulfate.

Toxicological studies

Gardenia (Genipin) Blue The Committee noted that the acute toxicity of Gardenia Blue polymer was low. The oral lethal dose (LD50) was more than 16 g/kg in mice and more than 10 g/ kg in rats (88).

text:
Gardenia (Genipin) Blue The Committee noted that the acute toxicity of Gardenia Blue polymer was low. The oral lethal dose (LD50) was more than 16 g/kg in mice and more than 10 g/ kg in rats (88).

The sponsor submitted several unpublished oral toxicity studies conducted with test materials with a Gardenia Blue polymer content of 24.7% or 32.3%. The Committee concluded that the test materials used in the studies were representative of the article of commerce. These studies evaluated various toxicological end-points, including short- and long-term oral toxicity, genotoxicity, and reproductive and developmental toxicity. In most studies, blue discoloration of faeces and some tissues, including kidneys, was observed in exposed animals. The Committee considered this finding to be treatment related but not adverse, as this observation was not associated with any histopathological changes. This conclusion was further supported by additional toxicological studies submitted by the sponsor that showed that the discoloration of kidneys observed in rats upon prolonged oral exposure was reversible upon discontinuation of exposure (89).

The Committee did not identify any treatment-related adverse effects in the evaluated short- and long-term oral toxicity studies conducted with Gardenia (Genipin) Blue, and the NOAEL was the highest dose tested in each study. The NOAELs of Gardenia (Genipin) Blue from these studies expressed in terms of the Gardenia Blue polymer content are provided in Table 3.4 (90–93).

This conclusion was further supported by additional toxicological studies submitted by the sponsor that showed that the discoloration of kidneys observed in rats upon prolonged oral exposure was reversible upon discontinuation of exposure (89).

The Committee did not identify any treatment-related adverse effects in the evaluated short- and long-term oral toxicity studies conducted with Gardenia (Genipin) Blue, and the NOAEL was the highest dose tested in each study. The NOAELs of Gardenia (Genipin) Blue from these studies expressed in terms of the Gardenia Blue polymer content are provided in Table 3.4 (90–93).

text:
The Committee also evaluated a 26-week oral toxicity study in transgenic ras-H2 mice (94) conducted with Gardenia (Genipin) Blue at doses of up to

- 10 440 mg/kg bw per day in the diet. No increased tumour incidences were found in these mice that were highly susceptible to accelerated tumour development. The Committee considered this study as supporting evidence for the conclusion that Gardenia (Genipin) Blue does not exhibit a potential for carcinogenicity. The Committee evaluated study reports of a bacterial reverse mutation assay (95), an in vitro chromosome aberration assay (96), an in vitro micronucleus assay (97), an in vivo erythrocyte micronucleus or Comet assay (98), an in vivo reverse Comet assay (98) and an in vivo Pig-a mutation assay (99) conducted with Gardenia (Genipin) Blue, all of which were negative. The Committee did not therefore identify a concern for genotoxicity of Gardenia (Genipin) Blue. The Committee evaluated reports of three reproductive and developmental toxicity studies conducted with Gardenia (Genipin) Blue: an extended one-generation reproductive toxicity study in rats (100), a prenatal developmental toxicity study in rats (101) and a prenatal developmental toxicity study in rabbits (102). No treatment-related adverse effects were observed in these studies. The Committee identified NOAELs of 3915 mg/kg bw per day, corresponding to the Gardenia Blue polymer content of 1264 mg/kg bw per day (100) and 2000 mg/kg bw per day (101,102), the highest doses tested. The sponsor submitted a study that analysed the presence of residual allergens in Gardenia (Genipin) Blue from the use of soy protein hydrolysates as a raw material in its formation (103). The Committee noted that there was no soy protein detected in the test material.

Geniposide and genipin The Committee evaluated toxicological data on geniposide and genipin and noted that the oral LD50 values for geniposide and genipin were 1431 mg/kg bw in rats and 510 mg/kg bw in mice, respectively (104).

A 90-day oral toxicity study of geniposide in rats did not report any treatment-related adverse effects at doses of up to 73 mg/kg bw per day (104). In a 26-week oral toxicity study of geniposide in rats at doses of up to 100 mg/kg bw per day (105), there were significant increases (P < 0.05) in some biochemical and haematological parameters, as well as liver and spleen weights, accompanied by histopathological changes in the liver and kidneys, in the high-dose group compared with controls. The Committee therefore identified the middle dose,

- 50 mg/kg bw per day, as the NOAEL for this study. Data from a 21-day oral toxicity study of genipin in mice showed hepatoxic effects at a dose of 100 mg/kg bw per day (106). The Committee identified the low dose, 50 mg/kg bw per day, as the NOAEL for this study. No longer-term oral toxicity studies on genipin were available.

Based on negative results in bacterial reverse mutation, Rec and sister chromatid exchange (SCE) assays conducted with geniposide, the Committee did not identify a concern for genotoxicity of geniposide (107).

text:
Based on negative results in bacterial reverse mutation, Rec and sister chromatid exchange (SCE) assays conducted with geniposide, the Committee did not identify a concern for genotoxicity of geniposide (107).

Genipin tested negative in bacterial reverse mutation assays (103,107), but showed a positive or equivocal response in several in vitro genotoxicity studies, including in vitro chromosome aberration (108), in vitro micronucleus (109), in vitro Comet (110), Rec (107) and SCE assays (107). The Committee noted that genipin tested negative in in vivo erythrocyte micronucleus and Comet assays, conducted using blood and tissues (stomach, duodenum and livers), respectively, from mice that were collected following oral exposure to genipin at doses of up to 222 mg/kg bw per day for 3 days (111). The Committee noted that this study was conducted according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Test Guideline No. 474 (112) and United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Redbook (113) test guidelines, and showed that there were no genotoxic effects of genipin in vivo. As stated above, the Committee noted that any genipin potentially formed in the body following oral exposure to geniposide would be rapidly conjugated before it reaches the systemic circulation. The Committee therefore concluded that no free genipin would be available to interact with DNA. The Committee did not identify a concern for genotoxicity of genipin in vivo.

Observations in humans

No data on observations of exposure to Gardenia (Genipin) Blue in humans were available.

Assessment of dietary exposure

section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)

3.1.6 Gardenia (Genipin) Blue
text:
The Committee reviewed the dietary exposure estimates to Gardenia (Genipin) Blue submitted by the sponsor that were based on adjusted maximum use levels at GMP combined with food consumption data from Brazil, Japan, the United Kingdom and the USA, as well as estimates based on the EFSA Comprehensive Database and CIFOCOss food consumption data. The Committee also calculated the high dietary exposure estimates using the mean dietary exposure for Japan. The mean and high dietary exposure estimates were up to 9.0 mg/kg bw per day and 13.8 mg/kg bw per day in children, and up to

- 3.7 mg/kg bw per day and 10.4 mg/kg bw per day for adults, respectively. Based on the highest dietary exposure for Gardenia (Genipin) Blue of
- 13.8 mg/kg bw per day, and considering the maximum Gardenia Blue polymer content of up to 36% from the specifications, the Committee calculated a dietary exposure expressed on the blue polymer basis of up to 5.0 mg/kg bw per day for children. Based on the specifications of geniposide in the article of commerce of 80 mg/kg, the Committee calculated a theoretical high dietary exposure to geniposide of 1 µg/kg bw per day. The Committee concluded that the conservative estimate of high exposure of 5.0 mg/kg bw per day for children should be considered in the safety assessment for Gardenia Blue polymer.

Evaluation

The Committee evaluated several reports of toxicological studies submitted by the sponsor to evaluate the safety of Gardenia (Genipin) Blue for the first time. The Committee noted that the test materials used in all the evaluated studies were representative of the article of commerce.

The Committee concluded that Gardenia Blue polymer is poorly absorbed upon oral exposure and extensively eliminated unchanged in the faeces.

3.1.7 Glycolipids
text:
Explanation

Glycolipids are found in membranes of various organisms. The article of commerce, also referred to as “IMD AM-1” or “AM-1”, referred to throughout as IMD AM-1, consists of structurally related glycolipids obtained from fermentation of the jelly mushroom Dacryopinax spathularia.

At its Fifty-third session, the CCFA requested an evaluation of the safety of glycolipids (71). Glycolipids have not previously been evaluated by the Committee.

Glycolipids are approved as a preservative in non-alcoholic beverages in Australia and New Zealand, Canada and the European Union. In the USA, glycolipids have Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) status when used as an antimicrobial agent in non-alcoholic beverages.

The Committee evaluated the submitted data, which included studies on pharmacokinetics, acute and short-term toxicity, long-term toxicity and carcinogenicity, genotoxicity, reproductive and developmental toxicity, dietary exposure, and chemical and technical considerations. The Committee conducted a literature search on the safety of and dietary exposure to glycolipids. Five publications on its safety were considered relevant to the current evaluation.

Chemical and technical considerations

Glycolipids from Dacryopinax spathularia (glycolipids; CAS No. 2205009-17-0) are a mixture of congeners of long-chain glycolipids. They are obtained by fermentation of the non-toxigenic D. spathularia strain MUCL 53181.

Explanation

Glycolipids are found in membranes of various organisms. The article of commerce, also referred to as “IMD AM-1” or “AM-1”, referred to throughout as IMD AM-1, consists of structurally related glycolipids obtained from fermentation of the jelly mushroom Dacryopinax spathularia.

At its Fifty-third session, the CCFA requested an evaluation of the safety of glycolipids (71). Glycolipids have not previously been evaluated by the Committee.

Glycolipids are approved as a preservative in non-alcoholic beverages in Australia and New Zealand, Canada and the European Union. In the USA, glycolipids have Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) status when used as an antimicrobial agent in non-alcoholic beverages.

The Committee evaluated the submitted data, which included studies on pharmacokinetics, acute and short-term toxicity, long-term toxicity and carcinogenicity, genotoxicity, reproductive and developmental toxicity, dietary exposure, and chemical and technical considerations. The Committee conducted a literature search on the safety of and dietary exposure to glycolipids. Five publications on its safety were considered relevant to the current evaluation.

Chemical and technical considerations

Glycolipids from Dacryopinax spathularia (glycolipids; CAS No. 2205009-17-0) are a mixture of congeners of long-chain glycolipids. They are obtained by fermentation of the non-toxigenic D. spathularia strain MUCL 53181.

text: D. spathularia belongs to the phylum Basidiomycota, recognizable by its edible, orange-coloured, spatula-shaped fruiting bodies. The three primary glycolipid congeners (IMD-028835, IMD-026045 and IMD-027455) found in glycolipids from D. spathularia, shown in Fig. 3.2, are composed of a saturated C26 fatty acid backbone and a glucopyranosyl-(1"2)-xylopyranosyl-(1"2)-xylopyranosyl trisaccharide moiety. IMD-028835 and IMD-026045 have the same molecular weight and are typically present together at 40%; IMD-027455 is typically present at 29%. The minor glycolipid congeners differ primarily from the three major congeners by the presence and location of acyl units (typically acetate, isovalerate and, in some congeners, 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutarate) on the trisaccharide. Glycolipids are produced by aerobic submerged fermentation using glucose and autolysed yeast extract as feedstock. The downstream process includes filtration and microfiltration to remove mycelial cells, precipitation and washing with acidified water. The final product is a pasteurized, spray-dried beige to light brown powder. The entire process is performed in accordance with current GMP. The total glycolipid content is specified as not less than 93% on a dry weight basis. The remainder consists of protein (≤ 3%), fat (≤ 2%) and sodium (1.7–3.3%). Glycolipids are surfactants intended for use as a preservative in select non-alcoholic beverages. They exhibit antifungal activity against yeast and mould in food.

The main components of IMD AM-1 are three closely structurally related glycolipid congeners (Fig. 3.2). A series of pharmacokinetic and mass balance studies in rats with labelled and unlabelled glycolipids demonstrated that these intact lipid congeners are not absorbed. Instead, a proportion of the glycolipids is hydrolysed by intestinal microflora to their components, namely glucose, xylose, acetate, isovalerate and long-chain fatty acids (LCFA) (114–117). These normal components of the diet are readily absorbed, and any remaining unchanged glycolipids are eliminated in faeces (74–83%).

The oral bioavailability of two of the IDM AM-1 congeners (IMD-028835 and IMD-026045) was 0.01%, and 0.001% for IMD-027455.

The Committee identified a NOAEL of 1201 mg/kg bw per day. Male and female dogs were orally exposed to glycolipids at doses of 150, 500 or 1000 mg/kg bw per day for 90 days. The only test-item-related effect observed was a reduction in feed intake with a corresponding reduction in body weight gain (approximately 30% lower than controls) among female dogs exposed to glycolipids at 1000 mg/kg bw per day (122,123). Given the absence of any systemic exposure to glycolipids, the Committee considered that this observation was unlikely to be adverse and concluded that the NOAEL for this study was 1000 mg/kg bw per day, the highest dose tested. The Committee evaluated reports of two reproductive and developmental toxicity studies on glycolipids in rats. The reproductive toxicity was investigated in a two-generation study where glycolipids were administered daily to rats at doses of up to 1000 mg/kg bw per day for the F0 and F1 generations (124,125). There were no test-item-related effects on body weight, body weight gain, feed consumption or feed efficiency in the F0 generation in any of the groups. A lower mean body weight gain was observed in males in the 150, 500 and 1000 mg/kg bw per day groups during the first week of the F1 generation. No differences in body weight gain in these groups were observed throughout the remainder of the study. There were no test-item-related effects on feed consumption or feed efficiency in F1 males and females. A dose-related increase in the incidence of respiratory noises (rales) was observed for F0 and F1 males and females, but was not considered toxicologically relevant.

3.1.7 Glycolipids
text:
Observations in humans

No data on the effects of oral exposure to glycolipids in humans were available.

Assessment of dietary exposure

Glycolipids are currently not included in the GSFA. For the current meeting, the sponsor requested the use of glycolipids as an antimicrobial preservative in non-alcoholic beverages at maximum use levels ranging from 25 to 100 mg/kg. The Committee evaluated estimates of dietary exposure to glycolipids from these beverages based on the use levels as submitted by the sponsor for the United Kingdom and the USA. In addition, dietary exposure estimates were evaluated for Australia (131) and Europe (132).

High (P95) dietary exposure estimates of glycolipids could be up to

- 3.3 mg/kg bw per day for children aged 2–5 years in the USA and 1.3 mg/kg bw per day for adults in Europe. The Committee considered that these high estimates of dietary exposure were the most suitable estimates currently available for evaluating dietary exposure to glycolipids, as they include all beverages to which glycolipids may be added at the requested maximum use levels. However, the Committee acknowledged that it is highly unlikely that glycolipids will be added to all beverages and, even if added, may not be at the maximum use level. These estimates are therefore overestimates of the actual exposure to glycolipids through the consumption of non-alcoholic beverages.

Evaluation

The Committee evaluated toxicological studies submitted by the sponsor to assess the safety of glycolipids. The Committee noted that the test materials used in the toxicological studies were representative of the article of commerce.

The studies on glycolipids evaluated by the Committee included acute toxicity, short-term toxicity, genotoxicity, and reproductive and developmental toxicity. Adverse effects were not noted at any dose tested.
