text: - 2 to account for the temporary designation of the ADI, pending the submission of studies to elucidate the potential developmental and reproductive toxicity of rosemary extract. An additional uncertainty factor to account for the lack of a chronic toxicity study was not considered necessary, based on the absence of adverse effects in the short-term toxicity studies at doses up to and including the highest dose tested. At the Eighty-seventh meeting, the Committee evaluated a submitted study on the reproductive and developmental toxicity of an acetone-based rosemary extract and several relevant studies published after the Eighty-second meeting of the Committee. The Committee concluded that the new studies provided evidence for the absence of reproductive toxicity, but not for the absence of developmental toxicity. The Committee retained the temporary ADI of 0–0.3 mg/kg bw, pending the submission of studies on the developmental toxicity of rosemary extract and studies to elucidate whether the effects noted on rodent pup thyroid hormone levels can be replicated. Estimated mean and high-percentile dietary exposures to carnosic acid plus carnosol from use of rosemary extract as a food additive for all countries assessed based on typical use levels did not exceed the temporary ADI of 0–0.3 mg/kg bw, whereas the estimated dietary exposures for children from naturally occurring sources combined with food additive use were up to 0.42 mg/ kg bw per day, which exceeds the ADI. The Committee did not consider the exceedance of the ADI to be a safety concern since the temporary ADI was based on the highest dose tested in a short-term toxicity study in rats. Further, in the newly submitted reproductive and developmental toxicity screening study, no effects on reproductive toxicity or on parental animals were observed at 316 mg/ kg bw per day, the highest dose tested.

text: Rosemary extract was placed on the agenda of the present meeting at the request of the CCFA at its Fifty-fourth session (21) for a safety assessment to evaluate the developmental toxicity and the effects on rodent pup thyroid hormone levels. The Committee evaluated unpublished studies with rosemary extract submitted by the sponsor, including a prenatal developmental toxicity study, a study on thyroid hormone levels and liver enzyme induction in immature rats, and an in vitro study on the effects on liver enzymes. Chemical and technical considerations

No new information was submitted.

Biochemical aspects

Several new studies were available. An in vitro study showed that the absorption and transportation of carnosic acid across Caco-2 cell monolayers mainly involves passive diffusion (136). In mice, carnosic acid was found in several tissues after 7 days of oral gavage exposure, with the highest tissue concentration in the cecum followed by the colon, stomach, spleen and liver (136). Carnosol was rapidly absorbed (Cmax 30 min) and had a half-life of approximately 45 hours after a single oral administration in mice (137). This half-life for carnosol was longer than that reported after oral gavage administration of a rosemary extract in mice (t1/2 7.5 hours) (138) or in a study in rats with rosemary extract (t1/2 12–

- 14 hours) evaluated previously by the Committee (139). Carnosic acid was not detected at any timepoint, indicating that carnosol was not metabolized to detectable concentrations of carnosic acid. Following oral administration of a rosemary extract (containing 40% w/w carnosic acid and 5% w/w carnosol) to mice, carnosol and carnosic acid were both rapidly absorbed (Cmax < 15 min), but carnosic acid was eliminated more quickly than carnosol (t1/2 3.5 and 7.5 hours, respectively) (138).

text: Exposure to rosemary acetone extract (INS No. 392; 53.7% carnosic acid and 4.1% carnosol) induced the expression of CYP3A4 in three-dimensional (3D) spheroid cultures of human primary hepatocytes and induced the expression of the homologous genes Cyp3a11 and Cyp3a23/3a1 in 3D spheroid cultures of primary hepatocytes from mice and rats, respectively. In human primary hepatocytes, rosemary extract also induced expression of CYP1A1, CYP2C19 (although the induction was minor), UGT1A1 and UGT1A4 (140). This indicates that there could be species differences in enzyme induction following exposure to rosemary extract. Previously, hepatic enzyme induction was reported in primary cultures of human hepatocytes following exposure to carnosic acid, as evidenced by upregulation of CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 mRNA levels. The induced expression of CYP3A4 is also in line with the results of a previous in vitro luciferase reporter gene assay that showed that carnosol is an activator for hPXR, mPXR and rPXR, whereas carnosic acid is a potent agonist of both hPXR and mPXR, but not rPXR (139).

In baculosomes expressing individual human CYP isoforms, carnosol inhibited CYP1A2, CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 (other CYPs were not investigated) (137). Livers were collected from pups on PND 13 or after reaching sexual maturity. Any statistically significant increases (> 1.5-fold) in gene and protein expression were observed in the low-dose group only and were therefore not considered to be biologically relevant.

3.1.8 Rosemary extract
text:
The Committee previously reviewed a study in adult female rats in which minimal increases (about 1.5-fold) were observed in total hepatic microsomal P450 content and in levels of hepatic CYP2A, CYP2C11, CYP2E1 and CYP4A activity but not in CYP1A, CYP2B or CYP3A. The rats were treated with a supercritical carbon dioxide extract of rosemary (33% w/w carnosol plus carnosic acid content), at a dose equal to 195 mg/kg bw per day for 13 weeks (55). This enzyme induction was observed to be reversible following a 4-week treatment-free period. Elevated liver enzyme activity (glutathione-S-transferase and quinone reductase) was observed in mice and rats fed commercial extracts of rosemary in the diet at concentrations equivalent to up to 900 and 500 mg/kg bw per day for mice and rats, respectively, for 2–4 weeks, but not for carnosol (55).

Toxicological studies

Several additional toxicological studies were available. A hydro-ethanolic rosemary extract (carnosol and carnosic acid not specified) was of low acute oral toxicity in mice (LD50 > 5000 mg/kg bw) (143).

No adverse effects were observed in a 28-day oral repeat-dose toxicity study with some deviations from the OECD Test Guideline No. 407 (144) in rats, conducted with an ethanolic extract of powdered rosemary leaves (carnosic acid and carnosol content unknown) (145). The NOAEL of this study was 1000 mg/kg bw per day, the highest dose tested.

publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)
3.1 Toxicological and/or dietary exposure assessment, and specifications
3.1.8 Rosemary extract
text:
In a study designed to address the recommendations of the Committee at its Eighty-seventh meeting (133), the potential effects of rosemary extract (INS No. 392; acetone extract containing 53.7% carnosic acid and 4.1% carnosol) on thyroid hormone levels in immature rats were examined (147). Rosemary extract was administered to female rats at dietary concentrations of 0, 1800, 3000 or 4200 mg/kg (equal to 0, 83, 133 or 205 mg/kg bw per day of carnosol and carnosic acid) from GD 6 to GD 19, and at doses of 0, 800, 1300 or 1900 mg/kg (equal to 0, 72, 125 or 176 mg/kg bw per day of carnosol and carnosic acid) from GD 20 throughout lactation to account for increased feed intake during lactation. Blood samples were collected for analysis of triiodothyronine (T3), thyroxine (T4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) from subsets of pups on PND 4 (T3 and T4 only, because of small sample size), PND 13 and at termination (sexual maturation, PND 43 for males and PND 50 for females).

In the F1 generation, TSH levels were only statistically significantly decreased in males of the mid-dose group at PND 13. No differences were observed in TSH levels for female offspring at PND 13 or for male and female offspring at termination (TSH was not measured at PND 4). The Committee noted that there was a large variation in the TSH measurements. At PND 4 and at termination, there were no statistically significant differences in serum T3 and T4 levels between the treated and control groups.

In the F1 generation, TSH levels were only statistically significantly decreased in males of the mid-dose group at PND 13. No differences were observed in TSH levels for female offspring at PND 13 or for male and female offspring at termination (TSH was not measured at PND 4). The Committee noted that there was a large variation in the TSH measurements. At PND 4 and at termination, there were no statistically significant differences in serum T3 and T4 levels between the treated and control groups.

At PND 13, the mean T3 level in females in the high-dose group was statistically significantly lower by 16% compared with the controls. For male offspring, a smaller decrease of 6% was observed in the T3 level at the high dose, which was not statistically significant. T4 levels were reduced in F1 males (by 12%, 7% and 23% in the low-, mid- and high-dose groups, respectively; the high-dose reduction was statistically significant) compared with controls. In female offspring, statistically significant reductions in T4 levels were observed in all treated groups (of 12%, 13% and 24% in low-, mid- and high-dose groups, respectively) compared with controls. At termination, no statistically significant differences were observed for T3, T4 and TSH levels for either male or female offspring. Since the effect of rosemary extract on thyroid hormones was transient and not accompanied by thyroid weight changes, histopathological findings in the thyroid or effects on sexual maturation, the study author did not consider the changes to be adverse.

text: The Committee noted that for T4, this new study replicated the findings of the earlier study (135,148) evaluated previously by the Committee (139), in which similar dietary concentrations of rosemary extract were given (2100, 3600 or 5000 mg/kg feed). In this earlier study, dose-related and statistically significant reductions in T4 levels were seen in the F1 offspring on PND 13. In male F1 offspring, the mean T4 reductions were 5%, 17% and 27% in the low-, mid- and high-dose groups, respectively, compared with controls. In female F1 offspring, T4 reductions of 6%, 15% and 25% were observed in the low-, mid- and high-dose groups, respectively, compared with controls. All these reductions were statistically significant, except for in low-dose males. Similarly, in both studies, TSH and T3 were not affected in a dose-related manner. The consistent results from these studies (135,147,148) show that the decrease in serum T4 levels in pups at PND 13 is likely to be treatment related.

text: The classical thyroid inhibitor, propylthiouracil (PTU), and other chemicals known to affect the thyroid such as polybrominated diphenyl ethers, perchlorate, perfluorinated substances and triclosan, all reduce T4 levels in the dams as well as the pups when treatment is administered during gestation and lactation. Although TSH levels are often unaffected, the reductions in T4 are sustained throughout the treatment period (149) and are not transient as in the rosemary extract studies. In the study on rosemary extract evaluated previously by the Committee, paternal T4 levels were measured at termination and were unaffected by treatment (135,148). In the new prenatal developmental toxicity study (150), only females were treated and T3 and T4 levels measured at termination were unaffected.

text: Reductions in thyroid hormone levels, particularly during prenatal and/ or postnatal development, are cause for concern. If these reductions occur at a specific stage of brain development, they may have an adverse effect. For example, in a publication by O’Shaughnessy et al. (151) using PTU as a thyroid inhibitor, a 40% decrease in pup serum T4 on PND 14 was estimated to equate to a 70% decrease in pup brain T4. However, the magnitude, duration and timing of T4 changes required to produce neurodevelopmental effects are not yet clear (152). There are several mechanisms by which T4 may be reduced. In the absence of a clear effect on TSH levels and on thyroid weights and histopathology, decreases in T4 could be caused by induction of liver enzymes, resulting in greater clearance of T4, rather than via a direct effect on the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis. In rats, the metabolism of thyroid hormones is mainly by phase II liver enzymes, UGTs (specifically UGT1A1 and UGT1A6) and sulfotransferases (SULTs). In the in vitro study by Anonymous (140) using primary rat hepatocyte cultures, rosemary extract induced protein expression of UGT1A1 but not UGT1A6, and did not induce gene expression for any of the UGT1A enzymes. The Committee also noted that no increases in liver weight or histopathological changes in the liver were observed in pups in that study, and that no clear effects were observed in CYP activity and protein expression in pups (142). Other possible mechanisms were not investigated. The mechanism and toxicological relevance of the transient reductions in T4 levels on PND 13 therefore remains unclear. In the absence of studies on neurodevelopmental toxicity, the Committee noted that this transient reduction in T4 levels could possibly lead to adverse neurodevelopmental effects. The Committee performed dose–response modelling on the pup T4 levels at PND 13 (see section on “Dose–response analysis” below). Additional studies in pigs, rats and hyperthyroid rats were identified from the literature search (153–156). These were considered less relevant for the safety evaluation of rosemary extract as a food additive because of the test materials used and/or the study design.

Observations in humans

No new data relevant to the evaluation of rosemary extract as a food additive were available.

Assessment of dietary exposure

Dose–response analysis

The Committee performed benchmark dose modelling using the individual data on pup T4 serum levels at PND 13 from the Anonymous (147) study. Ideally, a numerical benchmark response (BMR) is chosen that would reflect the onset of an adverse effect relevant to humans. EFSA (158) has used a BMR of 20% for decreases in maternal T4 levels based on changes resulting in neurodevelopmental effects in humans and in rat offspring, citing the following studies. publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)
3.1 Toxicological and/or dietary exposure assessment, and specifications
3.1.8 Rosemary extract
text:
Evaluation

No maternal or embryo-fetal toxicity was observed in a new prenatal developmental toxicity study in rats. A separate new study on thyroid hormone levels in rat pups from dams treated with rosemary extract in the diet during pregnancy and lactation confirmed the results of a previous study showing that rosemary extract exposure resulted in decreased serum T4 levels on PND 13 in male and female pups. A BMDL20 of 97 mg/kg bw per day expressed as carnosic acid plus carnosol was calculated for this study. This BMDL20 is higher than the NOAEL of 64 mg/kg bw per day, expressed as carnosic acid plus carnosol, on which the current temporary ADI for rosemary extract is based. This NOAEL of 64 mg/kg bw per day was the highest dose tested in a 90-day toxicity study in rats. The Committee considered that this NOAEL of 64 mg/kg bw per day is still the most appropriate point of departure, since higher doses of rosemary extract have only been tested in studies of reproductive and developmental toxicity of shorter duration and have not been tested in studies of chronic toxicity. In the derivation of the temporary ADI of 0–0.3 mg/kg bw per day, an additional uncertainty factor of 2 was incorporated into the overall uncertainty factor of 200 to account for the absence of studies to elucidate the potential developmental and reproductive toxicity of rosemary extract. This factor is no longer necessary. The temporary ADI of 0–0.3 mg/kg bw per day (expressed as carnosic acid and carnosol) was therefore withdrawn and an ADI of 0–0.6 mg/kg bw per day (expressed as carnosic acid and carnosol) was established.

3.1.8 Rosemary extract
text:
Estimated high dietary exposures to rosemary extract (expressed as carnosic acid plus carnosol) based on naturally occurring sources combined with dietary exposures from added sources at typical use levels were up to 0.84 mg/kg bw per day for children and up to 0.32 mg/kg bw per day for adults. The only adverse effect observed in reproductive and developmental toxicity studies in rats using higher doses was a reduction in T4 hormone levels in rat pups after exposure during pregnancy and lactation. The Committee therefore did not consider the slight exceedance of the ADI, which was only by children, as a safety concern. The Committee concluded that the use of rosemary extract as a food additive does not raise any safety concerns.

An addendum to the toxicological and dietary exposure monograph was prepared.

3.1.9 Thaumatin II
text:
Explanation

At its Fifty-fourth session, the CCFA requested that the Committee conduct a safety assessment of thaumatin II and, if necessary, to revise the specifications of thaumatin to include thaumatin II produced recombinantly in green plants such as spinach, lettuce, red beet and Nicotiana benthamiana (21).

Thaumatin II is one of the two major components of thaumatin (INS No. 957). Thaumatin is a mixture of intensely sweet proteins extracted with water from the arils of the fruit of the West African perennial plant Thaumatococcus daniellii (Benth). Thaumatin functions as a high-intensity sweetener and flavour enhancer.

Based on the information provided by the sponsor, the Committee evaluated thaumatin II produced by recombinant expression of the thaumatin II gene in transgenic lines of Nicotiana tabacum.

Thaumatin has previously been considered by the Committee at its Twenty-seventh and Twenty-ninth meetings (163,164). At its Twenty-ninth meeting (164), the Committee established an ADI “not specified”11 based on metabolism to normal food components and on a lack of adverse effects in toxicological and human studies.

No new toxicological studies on thaumatin or recombinant thaumatin II were submitted by the sponsor.

A literature search for the toxicity of thaumatin identified one new study that was relevant to the assessment. A literature search was also undertaken to identify publications that included concentration or use level data for thaumatin or estimates of dietary exposure to thaumatin. A small number of publications was identified and reviewed by the Committee.

- 11 The reader is referred to the Technical Report of the Eighty-seventh JECFA meeting for clarification of the term ADI “not specified”.

publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

3.1.9 Thaumatin II
text:
Genetic information

N. tabacum cultivar Burley B5 plants that are devoid of endogenous alkaloids, nicotine and anabasine are used as the host to produce thaumatin II in the seeds. A modified thaumatin II gene is inserted into the host DNA via Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transformation. This is accomplished with a plasmid carrying cassettes for the expression of DL-phosphinothricin resistance as a selection marker, and the expression of thaumatin II protein in the seeds. The presence of the thaumatin II transgene, genomic insertion sites and DNA copy number in the transformants was confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and DNA sequencing in the T0 and T1 generation candidates. The insertions were confirmed to be in different loci, and no tandem or inverted repeats were detected. Harvested T2–T3 generation plants were analysed to verify that there was no segregation of the transgene and then used for seed production by self-pollination. T4 generation seeds form the basis for plant propagation and thaumatin II production. The N. tabacum seeds are periodically assessed for germination rate, absence of pathogens, retention of genomic insertions and thaumatin II protein expression.

section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)

3.1.9 Thaumatin II
text:
Characterization of thaumatin

Thaumatin (INS No. 957) is a 2:1 mixture of thaumatin I and thaumatin II. The chemistry and applications of thaumatin have been extensively reviewed (165– 172). The proteins share similar properties, amino acid composition, sweetness and molecular weight (of about 22 kDa), only differing by five amino acids. Each consists of a single polypeptide chain of 207 amino acids with eight intramolecular disulfide bonds (170). X-ray crystallography studies of thaumatin I and II have elucidated their backbone structure (166,173,174). Circular dichroism analysis of thaumatin I (175) indicated a few α-helices, but numerous β-pleated sheets and bends. Disruption as a result of heat denaturation or cleavage of disulfide bonds leads to a loss of sweetness, suggesting that the tertiary structure of both the proteins is essential for taste modulation (167,176,177).

Characterization of thaumatin II

The amino acid sequence of seed-expressed thaumatin II is identical to that from

T. daniellii. The thaumatin II article of commerce is an odourless, white to off-white powder that is highly water soluble (> 20% w/v) and 3000–10 000 times sweeter than sucrose (178). The amino acid sequence and molecular mass were verified to match that of a thaumatin II working standard by four different analytical methods, namely: (i) capillary gel electrophoresis (CGE); (ii) matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization (MALDI) time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MS);
(iii) in-source decay (ISD) MS; and (iv) tryptic MALDI MS peptide mapping.

publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)

3.1.9 Thaumatin II
text:
The average molecular masses determined by MALDI MS matched the values in reference databases. Results from ISD-MS analysis of thaumatin II confirmed the mass of the protein to be 22 287 Da, and the lack of truncations or terminal modifications. MALDI MS of the tryptic digest of purified thaumatin II confirmed that accessory sequences and the signal peptide were cleaved to yield the expected mature protein. In totality, the average molecular mass of 22 287 ± 21.5 Da from these methods matches the values in the literature (179,180) for thaumatin II from T. danielli (22 293 Da).

The purity of thaumatin II was confirmed by CGE and HPLC to be 95.1– 96.3% and 95.4–97.2%, respectively.

Chemical and technical considerations

The tobacco plants expressing thaumatin II in the seeds are grown using standard agricultural methods (181), then harvested and cleaned according to current Good Agricultural and Collection Practices (182). The seeds are crushed and cold-pressed to remove the oil. The defatted seed cake is treated with an acid solution (pH < 4.5) to remove host proteins and other seed components. The thaumatin II in the resultant supernatant is further purified by salt precipitation and multiple filtration steps. The article of commerce is stabilized and standardized with food-grade ingredients; it is either spray-dried or lyophilized as a dry, white to off-white powder.

text:
The tobacco plants expressing thaumatin II in the seeds are grown using standard agricultural methods (181), then harvested and cleaned according to current Good Agricultural and Collection Practices (182). The seeds are crushed and cold-pressed to remove the oil. The defatted seed cake is treated with an acid solution (pH < 4.5) to remove host proteins and other seed components. The thaumatin II in the resultant supernatant is further purified by salt precipitation and multiple filtration steps. The article of commerce is stabilized and standardized with food-grade ingredients; it is either spray-dried or lyophilized as a dry, white to off-white powder.

The total protein content for the article of commerce is determined by colourimetry, using the Bradford assay and a bovine serum albumin standard. Biochemical aspects

In studies previously reviewed by the Committee, thaumatin was digested more rapidly than egg albumin in vitro by proteolytic enzymes (trypsin, chymotrypsin, peptidase) (183). A nitrogen balance study conducted in rats showed that the digestibility of thaumatin was similar to that of egg albumin; the majority of thaumatin proteins (90%) are metabolized and absorbed similarly to other dietary proteins (184).

Toxicological studies

The toxicological database for thaumatin was considered relevant to the evaluation of the safety of thaumatin II produced recombinantly in N. tabacum. With the exception of one 13-week study in rats, the studies were evaluated by the previous Committee. Additional details of these studies were provided in the published review of Higginbotham et al. The oral LD50 of thaumatin was more than 20 000 mg/kg bw in mice and rats (183,184).

publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)

3.1.9 Thaumatin II
text:
The oral LD50 of thaumatin was more than 20 000 mg/kg bw in mice and rats (183,184).

In a 13-week rat study the NOAEL was 3.0% w/w in the diet, the highest concentration tested (equal to 2417 mg/kg bw per day) (183,184). In a 13-week dietary study in rats not previously evaluated by the Committee (185), no adverse effects were observed at the highest concentration of 3.0% w/w in the diet (equal to 2502 mg/kg bw per day). In a 13-week dog study the NOAEL was 3% in the diet, the highest concentration tested (equal to 1400 mg/kg bw per day).

No long-term or carcinogenicity studies were available. Thaumatin was not mutagenic in a bacterial reverse mutation test at concentrations of up to 50 mg/plate or in a dominant-lethal assay in mice at doses of up to 2000 mg/kg bw per day (183,184). Although these studies evaluated the potential for mutagenicity and did not address other genotoxicity end-points (e.g. clastogenicity), the Committee noted that thaumatin is readily digestible to normal food components for which genotoxic properties would not be anticipated.

No new studies were available for reproductive and developmental toxicity. No effects were observed on testis, uterus or ovaries in short-term repeat-dose toxicity studies (183–185). The NOAEL in a developmental toxicity study in rats evaluated by the previous Committee was 2000 mg/kg bw per day, the highest dose tested.

Bioinformatics analysis conducted by the sponsor on the amino acid sequence for thaumatin II did not identify any matches with known allergens. The Committee noted that thaumatin is quickly degraded by digestive enzymes.

The Committee noted that most of the residual tobacco seed proteins present are common to other plant species consumed in the human diet. Additionally, no adverse effects were observed in rats, pigs or lambs consuming tobacco seeds as feed (186–189).

Observations in humans

In a clinical study evaluated by the previous Committee, no treatment-related changes were observed on haematological and blood biochemistry parameters in volunteers that consumed 280 mg thaumatin daily for 13 consecutive weeks (183,184). The previous Committee noted that no reactions to thaumatin were detected with skin prick testing after 14 days of oral administration of 100 mg/ day of thaumatin (183,184).

Assessment of dietary exposure

A dietary exposure assessment for thaumatin had not previously been undertaken by the Committee. The Committee evaluated information on use levels and dietary exposure that was submitted for consideration and obtained through a literature search. For the purposes of this assessment, where the food additive reviewed was referred to as thaumatin, it was assumed that the information was equally relevant to thaumatin II.

doc_title: Evaluation of certain food additives: one-hundredth report of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (WHO Technical Report Series 1058)
publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)
3.1 Toxicological and/or dietary exposure assessment, and specifications
3.1.9 Thaumatin II
text:
A dietary exposure assessment for thaumatin had not previously been undertaken by the Committee. The Committee evaluated information on use levels and dietary exposure that was submitted for consideration and obtained through a literature search. For the purposes of this assessment, where the food additive reviewed was referred to as thaumatin, it was assumed that the information was equally relevant to thaumatin II.

Thaumatin is permitted for use as a flavour enhancer and sweetener in the GSFA and in many countries. It is commonly permitted for use under conditions of GMP in a range of food categories including beverages, table-top sweeteners, confectionery, chocolate and cocoa products, food supplements, fruit and vegetable products, dairy products, condiments and sauces. Evaluation of the use of thaumatin via food product databases or label surveys from Australia, Brazil, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea and Europe shows that a small proportion of food products that are on the world-wide market contain the sweetener. It is most commonly found in table-top sweeteners, with other uses in beverages and confectionery and in lower proportions of snack bars, desserts, meal replacements and supplements.

Estimates of dietary exposure to thaumatin from the Republic of Korea based on poundage data, and from the USA and Europe based on individual dietary records, were reviewed by the Committee at the current meeting. For the evaluation, dietary exposures based on a range of foods containing thaumatin at maximum permitted levels (except for a use level for table-top sweeteners) could be for mean exposures up to 0.07 mg/kg bw per day for children and 0.05 mg/ kg bw per day for adults, and for high exposures up to 0.33 mg/kg bw per day for children and 0.27 mg/kg bw per day for adults.

Major contributors to dietary exposure when a range of foods were included in the assessment included food supplements for children (excluding infants and toddlers) and adults, flavoured drinks and confectionery for children, and table-top sweeteners for adults.

Evaluation

Thaumatin consists primarily of thaumatin I and thaumatin II proteins (in a ratio of 2:1) together with minor amounts of plant constituents. These proteins have similar properties, amino acid composition, sweetness and molecular weight (of about 22 kDa), and only differ by five amino acids. The amino acid sequence of thaumatin II produced by recombinant methods in Nicotiana tabacum is identical to that of thaumatin II extracted from the arils of the fruit of Thaumatococcus daniellii. On this basis, the toxicological database for thaumatin was considered relevant to the evaluation of the safety of thaumatin II produced recombinantly in N. tabacum.

At its Twenty-ninth meeting, the previous Committee established an ADI “not specified”12 for thaumatin (INS No. 957) obtained from T. daniellii.

One new 13-week toxicity study in rats was available for thaumatin that supports the previous evaluation. The NOAEL was 3.0% w/w in the diet, equal to 2502 mg/kg bw per day, the highest dose tested.

Based on the amino acid sequence similarity of thaumatin I, thaumatin II and recombinant thaumatin II, the Committee revised the ADI “not specified” for thaumatin (INS No. 957) to a group ADI “not specified” including thaumatin (INS No. 957) and thaumatin II produced by recombinant methods in the seeds of the tobacco plant N. tabacum.

3.2 Specifications of identity and purity
3.2.6 Gellan gum
text:
Gellan gum was on the agenda of the present meeting for the revision of specifications.

At its Eighty-seventh meeting the Committee was asked to consider the use of gellan gum in FSMP intended for infants and liquid fortification products for addition to human milk or infant formula. It was determined at that meeting that only low-acyl clarified gellan gum was used in these products. The Committee at its Eighty-seventh meeting concluded that “the MOE of 7.7 calculated for the use of gellan gum in FSMPs and liquid fortification products for addition to human milk or infant formula at a maximum level of 50 mg/L in the fed product indicates low risk for the health of infants, including preterm infants, and that its proposed use is therefore of no safety concern. This conclusion applies only to the use of low-acyl clarified gellan gum” (133). The Committee also retained the previously established ADI “not specified”16 for the general population.

Furthermore, the Committee (133) made the previously prepared specifications tentative pending the submission of (i) new methods for characterizing the three commercial forms of gellan gum (i.e. high-acyl, low-acyl and low-acyl clarified), (ii) a method to determine the degree of acylation of gellan gum, (iii) validation data for the submitted methods and (iv) data from five non-consecutive commercial batches for the three commercial forms of gellan gum.

At the Fifty-fourth session of the CCFA, separate INS numbers were established for gellan gum (INS No. 418(i)) and for low-acyl clarified gellan gum (INS No. 418(ii)) (21).

doc_title: Evaluation of certain food additives: one-hundredth report of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (WHO Technical Report Series 1058)
publisher: World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
section_path: 3. Specific food additives (other than flavouring agents)
3.2 Specifications of identity and purity
3.2.6 Gellan gum
text:
At the Fifty-fourth session of the CCFA, separate INS numbers were established for gellan gum (INS No. 418(i)) and for low-acyl clarified gellan gum (INS No. 418(ii)) (21).

At the current meeting, the Committee reviewed the new methods and data submitted for the characterization of the three forms of gellan gum. An HPLC method was submitted to differentiate high-acyl- from low-acyl-content gellan gum. A Kjeldahl nitrogen determination method was proposed to differentiate clarified from non-clarified gellan gums. The use of both methods was proposed to enable the characterization and differentiation of the three commercial forms of gellan gum.

- 17 The reader is referred to the Technical Report of the Eighty-seventh JECFA meeting for clarification of the term ADI “not specified”.

Incorporating the proposed methods allowed the Committee to generate new specifications for low-acyl clarified gellan gum (INS No. 418(ii)). The Committee also specified limits for arsenic (0.5 mg/kg), cadmium (0.5 mg/kg), lead (0.5 mg/kg) and mercury (0.1 mg/kg) based on its use for foods intended for infants.

The Definition in the existing specifications monograph for gellan gum (INS No. 418(i)) was updated to include any gellan gum, independent of the degree of acylation, not intended for use in foods for infants. The tentative status was removed.

The chemical and technical assessment for gellan gum was updated.

section_heading: 4.1 Maximum permissible lead levels in formula
text:
The Committee noted that at its Eighty-second meeting there was a decision to reduce the maximum permissible lead level in the specifications for carob bean gum and carob bean gum (clarified) when used in infant formula from 2 mg/ kg to 0.5 mg/kg. The current specifications were revised to include the following statement: “Not more than 0.5 mg/kg for use in infant formula and formula for special medical purposes intended for infants” (Table 4.1).
